title: Foreign Investors Just Poured a Record $3 Billion Into Indian Bonds in a Single Month. The Tax Break Worked.
excerpt: New Delhi scrapped capital gains and withholding taxes on government securities. In three weeks, foreigners bought almost twice what they had in the previous five months combined. Now Bloomberg is watching.
body:
India's gamble on tax reform just paid off faster than anyone expected.

Foreign investors bought a record $3 billion of Indian government bonds in June through the Fully Accessible Route, according to clearing house data released Tuesday. That is nearly double the $1.7 billion they purchased in the entire January-to-May period.

The surge was triggered by a sweeping set of policy measures rolled out earlier this month. New Delhi exempted foreign portfolio investors from the 12.5 percent long-term capital gains tax on government securities and scrapped a 20 percent withholding tax on bond interest income. The Reserve Bank of India simultaneously broadened the pool of securities eligible under the Fully Accessible Route to include longer-dated sovereign debt.

"The removal of taxation on Indian government bonds will mechanically make them more interesting for global investors and will help redirecting flows towards the onshore market," said Niel Clement, a portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

## The Bloomberg Index Play

The inflows are not just about yield. They are about inclusion.

India has been trying to break into the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index — one of the most influential fixed-income benchmarks in the world, tracked by trillions of dollars in assets. Bloomberg Index Services began soliciting investor feedback on Indian inclusion last September. The tax regime was one of the biggest operational frictions cited by potential investors.

Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages roughly $5.6 trillion, said inclusion now appears to be on the horizon. "Removing the tax element will ease some of the operational frictions for investors," Taylor said.



> **""Removing the tax element will ease some of the operational frictions for investors," Taylor said."**


India was already added to JPMorgan's Government Bond Index-Emerging Markets in June 2024, followed by FTSE Russell and Bloomberg's own emerging market indexes. The Global Aggregate is the big prize — it would force passive funds tracking the benchmark to allocate to Indian debt automatically, pulling in billions more.

## Oil, Rupee, and Goldman

The bond story does not exist in isolation. It is part of a broader quarter-end turnaround that has reshaped the outlook for Indian assets.


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


Brent crude tumbled over 20 percent in June, retreating to about $73 a barrel from the quarter's highs above $120, driven by the fragile US-Iran ceasefire and easing Hormuz disruptions. For oil-import-dependent India, the relief has been transformative.

The rupee logged its first quarterly gain since March 2025, ending Tuesday at 94.66 per dollar. Earlier in the quarter, the currency had fallen to record-low levels near 97 in May before recovering to become one of Asia's best performers in June.

Goldman Sachs has revised its India outlook upward, raising its 2026 growth forecast by 30 basis points, lowering its inflation projection by 20 basis points, and now projecting a balance of payments surplus of 0.7 percent of GDP. In March, the same bank had slashed India's growth forecast to 5.9 percent and warned of rate hikes.

"The reforms are bearing fruit, with inflows picking up," said Lavanya Venkateswaran, executive director and senior ASEAN and India economist at OCBC Bank.

## The Bigger Picture

The June bond rush is the most visible result of a coordinated policy blitz that New Delhi launched to stabilise the rupee and shore up external balances strained by the oil shock. Beyond the tax exemptions, the government introduced incentives for banks to raise foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians and for companies to tap overseas borrowings.

The RBI extended a subsidised forex swap facility for lenders' overseas borrowings and allowed banks to lend to non-residents against foreign-currency deposits. Some analysts estimate the combined measures could draw as much as $50 billion in inflows.

But the quarter ended on a cautious note. Indian benchmark indices fell on Tuesday as IT stocks dragged on concerns that US interest rates could stay higher for longer. The Nifty 50 dropped 0.34 percent to 23,865.75 and the Sensex fell 0.33 percent to 76,478.67, though both posted monthly gains for June.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, the quarter's developments cut several ways. The rupee's recovery from near-97 to 94.66 affects the value of every remittance. The new FCNR deposit schemes — offering rates near 7 percent — have already triggered a frenzy among banks targeting NRI dollar deposits. And the bond tax exemptions, while aimed at institutional investors, signal a broader opening of India's debt markets that could eventually extend to retail NRI participation.

The question is whether this is the beginning of sustained reform or a crisis-driven reflex that fades when oil prices stabilise. For now, the money is moving.

*Sources: Reuters, Press Information Bureau, Livemint, OCBC Bank, Goldman Sachs*
